implementation_notes: The idiomatic Python realization ties publication to the commit boundary instead of to a transactional queue: inside transaction.atomic() a call to transaction.on_commit(callback) runs the callback only after the outermost transaction commits and never on rollback; SQLAlchemy offers the equivalent through session events (after_commit) or a two-phase session, and other frameworks expose similar hooks. When a crash between COMMIT and the in-memory callback would lose the message, the callback is replaced by an outbox row written in the same transaction and published by a separate worker.
code_sketch:
with transaction.atomic():
    order = Order.objects.create(**payload)
    transaction.on_commit(lambda: producer.send("orders", order.event()))
# or, when the crash window between commit and callback must be closed:
with transaction.atomic():
    Order.objects.create(**payload)
    Outbox.objects.create(topic="orders", payload=json.dumps(payload))
pitfalls: on_commit callbacks live in memory: a process crash after COMMIT but before the callback runs loses the publication, so guarantees beyond best-effort need the outbox row plus a relay.
Callbacks registered inside a nested atomic() block run only at the outermost commit, and discarding them silently is a common way to lose events.
A publish call placed in the transaction body (rather than the hook) still races the commit: the broker can see the message while the transaction is still open.

variants.name: confluent-kafka transactional producer
variants.implementation_notes: The broker-side realization: a Producer configured with a stable transactional.id calls init_transactions() once, then begin_transaction(), produce(), optionally send_offsets_to_transaction() to commit consumed offsets, and commit_transaction() or abort_transaction(). It makes the broker operations atomic among themselves and gives exactly-once effects for consume-transform-produce, but it cannot include a database write, so database-coupled services combine it with an outbox row or with the commit-hook variant.
variants.code_sketch:
p = Producer({"bootstrap.servers": brokers, "transactional.id": "orders-0"})
p.init_transactions()
p.begin_transaction()
p.produce("orders", key=str(order_id), value=event)
p.send_offsets_to_transaction(consumer.position(consumer.assignment()),
                              consumer.consumer_group_metadata())
p.commit_transaction()          # or p.abort_transaction()
pitfalls: init_transactions() must be called exactly once per producer and the transactional.id must be stable, otherwise zombie fencing is lost.
A transactional producer cannot run two transactions concurrently and is not thread-safe; sharing it across threads or asyncio tasks breaks the transaction state.
A failed commit_transaction() aborts the transaction, so the retry path must re-initialise before reusing the producer.
